questions.topic: First-year audit of a chain — planning the engagement
o: Predecessor inquiry under the Code + acceptance/continuance evaluation including why the resignation happened
questions.why: Before any audit work, the incoming auditor must make the required written inquiry of the previous auditor (professional code) and weigh ethics/competence/capacity for acceptance — a resignation citing unverified receivables is exactly the fact pattern the acceptance check exists to process.

questions.topic: First-year audit of a chain — planning the engagement
questions.q: With two staff and eight weeks, the strategy should reflect:
o: Ignore capacity — do what is needed
Resource constraints shape scope depth (which components get direct testing vs reliance), staffing (add a specialist for ERP controls), and where PM tightens
questions.why: Strategy includes team composition, resources, and timing; a constraint this tight is handled by design (more ITGC reliance with specialist, targeted substantive depth), not by skipping mandatory work (counts, confirmations are procedures to design, not to delete when convenient — deleting without replacement is an evidence failure).
questions.trend: Fits the style in which ICAI drafts RTP/MTP questions on this topic (pattern estimate; no guarantee of appearance).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — this topic stays active in ICAI question-setting AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.ti: TI: First-year audit of a chain — planning the engagement
mem.tip: Capacity is a strategy input, never an excuse The schedule squeezes how you audit, never whether.

questions.topic: First-year audit of a chain — planning the engagement
questions.q: For the manual-franchisee receivables (2% of total, 15 counterparties):
o: Test all 15 (small population, high risk from the resignation history)
questions.why: Small, risky, individually checkable population ⇒ 100% testing is the cheap, complete answer — the prior-year audit file isn't evidence, and '2% of total' misses that the resignation reason concentrates risk there.

questions.topic: First-year audit of a chain — planning the engagement
questions.q: The client asks you to use last year's controls testing to save time. You should:
o: Use prior evidence only for non-significant-risk controls per the frequency rules, confirm the controls still exist, and test this year's significant-risk controls regardless
Rely only if the fee is cut
questions.why: SA 330 architecture: reliance on prior tests is permitted for controls not tied to significant risks (with the period rule and a confirmation of continued operation); significant-risk and ITGC-reliance controls get tested this year — the resignation history may even re-classify AR to significant.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — this topic stays active in ICAI question-setting Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

questions.topic: First-year audit of a chain — planning the engagement
questions.q: Overall materiality for this listed service business is best set by:
o: A benchmark (revenue, since the cafés are margin-thin and PBT swings) with the percentage tied to user focus, then PM below it
questions.why: Benchmark choice: what users watch — revenue is the stable base (PBT volatile in cafés); PM = haircut under OM for undetected error; size of the company or fee is irrelevant to the definition.

questions.q: The overall audit strategy differs from the audit plan in that it:
o: Lists the procedures for each assertion
Sets scope, timing and direction and guides the plan's development
questions.why: Strategy: characteristics, reporting objectives, engagement teams, significant considerations (scope, timing, direction); plan: the nature/timing/extent of procedures for each area — plan is the route map, strategy is the destination choice.
questions.trend: Repeated theme in recent ICAI exam question-patterns for this paper (AI pattern estimate — not a citation to a specific past paper question).
questions.probWhy: Realistic likelihood for Nov 2026 — strategy = direction; plan = the procedures that follow AI prediction, not a certainty.

mem.tip: An audit without strategy is a hike with better paperwork.
mem.link: Chapter 3 — Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution

questions.q: Discussing planning matters with those charged with governance:
o: Efficiently conducts the engagement by sharing understanding — the strategy remains the auditor's alone
Transfers responsibility for the audit to them
questions.why: Two-way discussion at planning is encouraged (logistics, knowledge) — but overall strategy and the audit plan remain the auditor's exclusive responsibility; discussing scope in detail may harm unpredictability, so it is general in nature.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — discuss with them; never hand them the pen Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

questions.q: Before detailed planning, the auditor undertakes activities including:
o: Considering acceptance/continuance, ethical requirements, and the engagement letter's terms
questions.why: Preliminary activities: policies for acceptance/continuance, confirming no misunderstanding with the predecessor (for changes), and the engagement letter defining scope and responsibilities — all precede the strategy.
questions.trend: No dominant past-pattern signal; included for balanced coverage (AI judgement).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — the engagement letter is a pre-plan contract, not a post-plan formality Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

questions.q: The first communication with the outgoing auditor on a new appointment should:
o: Be skipped if the client objects
Be made with the client's permission, asking about facts bearing on acceptance (including why the auditor left)
questions.why: The Code requires the prospective auditor to ask the predecessor about circumstances before accepting — the client's refusal to allow it is itself an answer.

questions.q: Before detailed planning, the auditor considers the engagement's reporting framework, entity's sector and ownership. This shapes:
o: The scope, applicable reporting regime and the relevant SAs/Laws to design around
questions.why: Preliminary understanding sets the perimeter: framework (Ind AS vs AS), statutory overlays (listing regulations, sectoral law), and the acceptability of the financial reporting framework is itself a first-step consideration.

questions.q: Aligning audit milestones with the client's reporting calendar is part of:
o: The overall strategy (timing) — drives interim work, cut-off tests, and review slots
questions.why: Timing is a strategy component: how much at interim vs year-end, when counts and confirmations run, and the report deadline that compresses all of it — mis-designed timing becomes an evidence gap at the finish.
questions.trend: Core concept that appears in some avatar in most attempts under the new scheme (pattern estimate).
questions.probWhy: Lower likelihood but possible — the calendar is an audit input Included so a low-probability surprise cannot catch you cold.

mem.tip: A missed date tests the auditor, not the client.
